title: PHE: supported ways to show the same thinking
subtitle: Six health companions and two reusable PE cue pages. Read, listen, point, speak, draw or write.

pages.title: A way back into the game
pages.goal: Change a barrier while respecting a boundary.
pages.start: Listen or read. Point, speak, draw or write. Fictional game: after a mistake, players must run a long loop. One player asks to walk a short return. The captain refuses. Someone starts pulling the player without asking. The goal is passing practice. Barrier: something blocking participation. Boundary: a limit to respect.

model.text: Example: A partner offers a hand. The learner says no. The partner accepts no and asks, "What would help?" Help needs permission.

tasks.prompt: Point to a rule or action blocking participation. What boundary matters?
tasks.answer: The compulsory long return or unasked pulling can block participation. Ask before touching and accept the response.

tasks.prompt: Choose or design one change. Show how passing practice continues.
tasks.answer: Accept a feasible change linked to the barrier. The player still has useful passing turns.

tasks.prompt: What could the group ask or notice to check whether the change helped?
tasks.answer: Player feedback and a no-name observation can support a decision; touches alone do not prove inclusion.

teacher.when: Use with Week 1 health, Boundaries and a way back in; offer alongside the original student page.
teacher.alignment: Same goal as w1-health: identify a participation barrier, respect consent and propose a practical change without losing the passing goal.
teacher.lookFor: A case detail, an accepted boundary, a workable redesign and a useful check. Accept supported alternatives; choice cards are starting points, not a single-answer test.
notes: Read the case, model and each choice aloud once while pointing; reread on request. Keep cards visible for pointing, speech or AAC. These are word cards with oral support, not independent pictorial access. Pause/help cues are the same across pages.
Read the supplied case/model aloud and offer pointing, speech, drawing, dictation, home language or AAC. No personal access explanation is required.
Do not role-play unwanted contact or simulate disability. A learner may pass on public sharing.
Keep task.answer in the teacher guide only. This page supports reasoning; it is not physical-skill evidence.

pages.title: Pause, choose, get support
pages.start: Listen or read. Point, speak, draw or write. Fictional case: a player misses two passes, grips the ball and says, "I cannot do this." They ask for a pause. A teammate wants to restart now. The teacher is busy.

model.text: Example: A drawing tears. The learner pauses, tries a quiet count, then asks an adult for help. A strategy can change; returning is not forced.

tasks.prompt: Point to a clue in the case. What should the teammate respect?
tasks.answer: The words, grip or pause request are observable. Respect the pause; do not diagnose the player.

tasks.prompt: Choose a first action and a strategy. Explain why they fit.
tasks.answer: Several safe plans fit. Connect the choice to the case; no strategy has to work for everyone.

tasks.prompt: The strategy does not help and the teacher is busy. Show a backup.
tasks.answer: Seek another available responsible adult. Do not pressure an immediate return or leave the learner without support.

teacher.when: Use with Week 2 health, Pause, choose a strategy, ask for help.
teacher.alignment: Same w2-health reasoning: notice a cue, protect a pause, choose a strategy/help route and retain a backup.
teacher.lookFor: A feasible plan with choice and support. Pointing to action cards plus an oral explanation is sufficient; a polished personal story is not needed.
notes: Read the case, model and each choice aloud once while pointing; reread on request. Keep cards visible for pointing, speech or AAC. These are word cards with oral support, not independent pictorial access. Pause/help cues are the same across pages.
Confirm actual available school adults and where to find them before the lesson. Keep this fictional; do not collect emotional histories.
The four original strategy choices are supplied on the page. Read them aloud; let learners choose or propose another safe strategy.
This is strategy practice, not diagnosis or a promise that counting resolves distress. Real concerns use school procedures.

pages.title: Change one part of a plan
pages.goal: Fit a movement plan to the available time and space.
pages.start: Listen or read. Point, speak, draw or write. Fictional case: the outdoor route is unavailable. A learner has ten minutes and a clear indoor space. Nothing needs buying. FITT: frequency = how often; intensity = how hard; time = how long; type = which activity.

model.text: Example: A five-minute walk becomes five minutes of seated reaching and tapping. Type changes; time stays. The learner can pause and adjust.

tasks.prompt: Choose an indoor activity. Why does it fit this case?
tasks.answer: Accept a feasible activity suited to the space/time. No route or body is ranked.

tasks.prompt: Name one FITT change. Add a private check and a rest, stop or help option.
tasks.answer: Connect a change to the constraint and include an adjustable check-in. A personal effort number is unnecessary.

tasks.prompt: Now only five minutes remain. Revise the plan and explain your choice.
tasks.answer: A shorter duration or another feasible activity can fit. Explain the change rather than prescribe a fitness target.

teacher.when: Use with Week 3 health, A realistic choice for today.
teacher.alignment: Same w3-health goal: connect one FITT change to a real constraint, include a private check-in, then adapt to a changed day.
teacher.lookFor: Accurate FITT language and a realistic plan with choice. Different activities can be equally defensible.
notes: Read the case, model and each choice aloud once while pointing; reread on request. Keep cards visible for pointing, speech or AAC. These are word cards with oral support, not independent pictorial access. Pause/help cues are the same across pages.
This page reasons about a fictional plan. Completing it does not demonstrate physical activity.
No body measures, effort scores, home activity reports or family equipment purchases are required.
Demonstrate unfamiliar words or movements only within an appropriate teacher-approved space and support plan.

pages.title: A claim needs evidence
pages.goal: Check a claim and protect private information.
pages.start: Listen or read. Point, speak, draw or write. Fictional ad: NeonFocus Gear sells PowerBand. "Everyone feels calm and scores better after seven days! Proof: 200 likes and one anonymous review. Post your face photo and daily energy score." No study is named. Source capsule: BC Women's Hospital + Health Centre (PHSA), Evaluating Online Health Info, paraphrased: check author, qualifications, purpose, review date and research. Start with established health organizations, such as HealthLink BC. This guidance does not test PowerBand. Claim = what a message says is true. Evidence = checkable information supporting a claim.

model.text: Example: An ad calls a shoe "best for every sport." I can identify the seller. I still need checkable evidence for that claim.

tasks.prompt: Point to the seller, the claim and the offered proof. What is missing?
tasks.answer: NeonFocus sells it; calmness/scores are claims. Likes/review are not checkable research. Relevant evidence is missing.

tasks.prompt: What does the real source help you check? What can it not prove?
tasks.answer: It guides source checks. It does not establish whether PowerBand works or fails.

tasks.prompt: Choose a safe next step. What stays private?
tasks.answer: Pause and seek reliable adult-supported information; do not post the requested photo or personal score.

frames: The claim is ___. We still need ___.

teacher.when: Use with Week 4 health, A confident claim is not enough.
teacher.alignment: Same w4-health thinking: source/purpose, claim/evidence, missing information, source limits and a privacy-safe response. Both student inputs are supplied offline.
teacher.lookFor: A distinction between a seller's claim, attention or anecdote, and relevant checkable evidence. Commercial purpose invites scrutiny; it is not automatic disproof.
notes: Read the case, model and each choice aloud once while pointing; reread on request. Keep cards visible for pointing, speech or AAC. These are word cards with oral support, not independent pictorial access. Pause/help cues are the same across pages.

Authentic capsule is a short paraphrase, not a fabricated study: BC Women's Hospital + Health Centre (PHSA), Evaluating Online Health Info: https://www.bcwomens.ca/health-info/staying-healthy/navigating-the-health-system/evaluating-online-health-info
Canadian Paediatric Society background for source/privacy checks: https://caringforkids.cps.ca/handouts/behavior-and-development/health_information_on_the_internet
Read the ad and capsule separately and label the ad fictional. No purchase, health disclosure, product experiment or internet access is required.
Keep answer text in teacher materials only; the different shoe example models a check without answering the full PowerBand task.

pages.title: Question the message; respect people
pages.goal: Challenge a body-rating message without judging bodies.
pages.start: Listen or read. Point, speak, draw or write. Fictional post: a sportswear seller calls an edited picture "the only athletic look" and invites body ratings. The small print says the image was edited. A group chat repeats the invitation. No real photograph is needed.

model.text: Example: A shoe seller says one shoe suits every sport. I ask which sports were tested. Selling something is a reason to check, not proof either way.

tasks.prompt: Which facts can the post support? Which personal judgments can it not establish?
tasks.answer: Sale/editing are supplied facts. The image cannot establish health or worth; do not rate anyone.

tasks.prompt: Replace the rating invitation with two welcoming lines. Explain one word choice.
tasks.answer: Accept respectful wording that welcomes different participation routes without ranking bodies or appearance.

tasks.prompt: Targeting continues. Choose a boundary or help response and explain it.
choices: Leave the chat and seek help
tasks.answer: Several safe responses fit. Include adult support if targeting continues; the targeted person is not to blame.

teacher.when: Use with Week 5 health, Respect bodies; question the message.
teacher.alignment: Same w5-health reasoning: notice constructed/commercial media, distinguish claims from what an image can establish, and use a respectful boundary/help route.
teacher.lookFor: A critical message response and practical wording. Do not confuse supportive agreement with evidence; learners can explain different defensible choices.
notes: Read the case, model and each choice aloud once while pointing; reread on request. Keep cards visible for pointing, speech or AAC. These are word cards with oral support, not independent pictorial access. Pause/help cues are the same across pages.
Background: MediaSmarts, Talking to Kids about Media and Body Image: https://mediasmarts.ca/teacher-resources/talking-kids-about-media-body-image-tip-sheet
Do not display or rate student bodies, ask for appearance concerns, or role-play insults. Use the supplied fictional description.
This is partial media/identity work, not complete puberty teaching. Personal concerns go privately through school support procedures.

pages.title: A help path with a backup
pages.goal: Protect first, get adult help and follow up.
pages.start: Listen or read. Point, speak, draw or write. Fictional message: an unknown account offers a sports-team place. It asks for a face photo, home address and private health details: "Keep this secret. Meet alone." The teacher will confirm where school helpers can be found.

model.text: Different case: a practice area is unsafe and someone is hurt. Move away from danger and alert the supervising adult now. Do not investigate or diagnose.

tasks.prompt: For the message case, choose protection now. Explain one choice.
choices: Do not reply or send details
Do not go to the meeting
tasks.answer: Avoid replying, sharing or meeting; seek adult support. Several protection actions can work together.

tasks.prompt: Choose a helper and confirmed place. Say or show a short help sentence. Who is the backup?
tasks.answer: Use an available adult/location, a brief request such as "I need help with a message", and another adult if needed.

tasks.prompt: What changes if there is immediate danger?
tasks.answer: Use adult/emergency help now, following school procedures. Do not delay for proof or a perfect explanation.

teacher.when: Use with Week 6 health, Protect first, get help, follow up.
teacher.alignment: Same w6-health goal: immediate protection, appropriate adult/location, backup and urgency. The model uses the other original low-detail case so the learner transfers the reasoning.
teacher.lookFor: Safety before investigation or evidence collection; responsibility placed with adults; a reachable backup. No personal disclosure is needed.
notes: Read the case, model and each choice aloud once while pointing; reread on request. Keep cards visible for pointing, speech or AAC. These are word cards with oral support, not independent pictorial access. Pause/help cues are the same across pages.
Before use, confirm actual school help roles/locations and the emergency route. Learners may point while the teacher records a role, never a classmate's private details.
Do not ask learners to confront an account, stage an emergency or gather risky evidence. They may use a different low-detail case or pass on public sharing.
Official support background: https://kidshelpphone.ca/ . For immediate danger use school emergency procedures or 911; non-emergency private support does not replace emergency help.

pages.title: Ready, send, receive, reset
pages.goal: Make the next pass playable and communicate clearly.
pages.start: Listen or read. Point, speak, draw or write. Use a teacher-taught partner activity. Teacher supplies safe space and suitable equipment. Fresh problem: both partners signal ready, but the ball keeps going beyond the receiver. Point, speak or draw a plan before practising.

model.text: Example: a receiver is not ready. The sender waits for a ready signal, then makes a gentle roll. The receiver controls it. They pause before the next turn.

tasks.prompt: For the fresh problem, choose one teacher-approved change. Why?
tasks.answer: Choose a change that could improve control. The ready signal alone does not solve every distance or force problem.

tasks.prompt: Practise three exchanges through your agreed movement route. Name what you actually used.
tasks.answer: Observe the actual taught skill. Catch/send is a useful bridge but is not a forearm-pass demonstration.

tasks.prompt: What changed? Show the agreed pause or help signal.
tasks.answer: Connect an observed difference to the adjustment; use the established safe stop/help routine.

teacher.when: Reuse in the six-week PE sequence, especially Weeks 1-2 passing and Weeks 4-6 light-ball practice.
teacher.alignment: Same physical and strategic goals: controlled sending/receiving, ready signals, safe pauses and evidence-based adjustment. This cue page does not introduce new technique or replace lesson rules.
teacher.lookFor: Physical control through a suitable movement route plus a reasoned cue/adjustment. Strategy explanations and physical demonstrations are separate evidence.
notes: Read the case, model and each choice aloud once while pointing; reread on request. Keep cards visible for pointing, speech or AAC. These are word cards with oral support, not independent pictorial access. Pause/help cues are the same across pages.
Teacher chooses the already-taught activity, equipment, clear lanes and stop signal. Keep the original no-contact, retrieval and supervision rules.
Offer purposeful seated/standing/wheeling movement, distance/ball adaptations and rest/return. No family equipment purchase is required.
A temporary observer can complete the planning/explanation. This does not demonstrate the physical skill; agree a suitable movement opportunity separately.
Do not require body data, comparison scores, a photograph or video.

Teach the shared cues aloud: Stop means follow the existing freeze signal and secure equipment safely; Pause requests rest and a chosen return; Help signals the teacher. Rehearse without turning a request into a public disclosure.

pages.title: Choose one change, then replay
pages.goal: Use clear instructions and evidence to improve familiar practice.
pages.start: Listen or read. Point, speak, draw or write. Fictional Gate Pass group: players crowd one gate and spend long periods waiting. They want safe passing turns and choices. Select only a change the teacher approves. Captains lead familiar practice while the teacher supervises.

model.text: Different example: two receivers chase one ball. The team agrees a receiving signal, replays, then checks whether space stayed clear. One observation does not settle every question.

tasks.prompt: Choose or design one change for the gate problem. Predict its effect.
tasks.answer: Accept a feasible change tied to crowding or waiting; preserve purposeful movement, choice and safety.

tasks.prompt: Give a short instruction for the changed game. Include a stop and return cue.
tasks.answer: Instructions must match the familiar teacher-approved rules. Captains do not remove support routes or invent safety rules.

tasks.prompt: After replay, choose a decision. Use one observation and player feedback.
tasks.answer: Several decisions can fit the evidence. Check safety, useful turns and choice; do not rank players.

teacher.when: Use during PE1 captain preparation or PE2 familiar practice in any of the six weeks.
teacher.alignment: Same everyone-in-game/strategy-remix thinking: notice a pattern, test one approved change, communicate and decide from evidence. Use the supplied gate case for planning or an actual familiar replay when feasible.
teacher.lookFor: Specific instructions, a reasonable prediction and a decision grounded in group evidence plus feedback. More touches alone do not establish choice or enjoyment.
notes: Read the case, model and each choice aloud once while pointing; reread on request. Keep cards visible for pointing, speech or AAC. These are word cards with oral support, not independent pictorial access. Pause/help cues are the same across pages.
Teacher approves equipment, space, rules and access, remains supervising and manages safety decisions. Rotate leadership jobs without removing movement turns.
Paper planning shows strategy/communication. An observer or captain explanation does not itself demonstrate physical performance; preserve a suitable movement route and assess it separately.
Use no-name observations only. No fitness rankings, body disclosures or public performance record is required.
The choice cards are response starters, not pre-approved rules for every space.

Teach the shared cues aloud: Stop means follow the existing freeze signal and secure equipment safely; Pause requests rest and a chosen return; Help signals the teacher. Rehearse without turning a request into a public disclosure.
